intro: Welcome to English at real speed! Films, series, podcasts and friends at a party don't speak like a textbook: they say 'dunno' and 'kinda', talk over each other and make jokes you can hear but not quite get. In this lesson you learn what to listen for, so that the hours you spend watching and listening in English turn into real understanding.
teachingNotes: Recap and build, one line each, don't re-teach: b2-pron-connected-speech taught elision ('las night'), assimilation ('tem people', 'doncha', 'wouldja'), weak forms and gonna/wanna/gotta with their limits (gonna only + a verb, never + a place; wanna not after she/he); c1-listening-implicit taught implied meaning (understatement, irony, reluctance, hedged refusals, faint praise), following panels (NAME = VIEW), self-corrections (the last version is the fact), asides and fillers to ignore; c1-world-englishes taught varieties as tendencies and clear English as a lingua franca. New at C2: more reduced forms, 'was gonna', vague language, quotatives, film slang by country, turn-taking in overlapping talk, and how to learn from films, series and stand-up.

BE HONEST ABOUT THE AUDIO: every recording in the app is ONE calm text-to-speech voice at normal speed, one speaker per clip. It cannot produce fast slurred speech, overlapping voices, accents or comedy timing, and the lesson says so. The app trains WHAT to listen for; real native-speed practice comes from the learner's own films, series and podcasts and from the resources. `listen` clips may contain gonna, wanna, kinda, dunno (a TTS reads them sensibly); lemme, gimme, whaddya, d'you, gotcha are taught and tested in text. Overlap is practised with written transcripts (— = cut off, … = trails away). Jokes are taught in text (… or | marks the pause). Never quote real films, series, songs or comedians: every joke and scene is an original practice text; real shows may only be named to explain a reference.

Fast colloquial speech: kinda = kind of, sorta = sort of, dunno = don't know, lemme = let me, gimme = give me, whaddya = what do you (sometimes what are you: whaddya doing?), d'you = do you, ya = you, y'know = you know, gotcha = I understand / got you, c'mon = come on, 'cause/cuz = because, very casual US 'Jeet?' = Did you eat? 'I was gonna…' = I planned to, but didn't (a 'but' usually follows). Fillers (like, you know, I mean, basically), vague language (and stuff, and that (UK), or whatever, or something, sort of, -ish: sevenish = about seven, a bunch of (US) = a lot of), quotatives (be like / go = say or react: 'and he's like, "Seriously?"'), literally as an intensifier. Slang by country: US I'm down = I'll join (NOT 'I'm feeling down' = sad), my bad = my mistake, bail (on) = cancel or leave suddenly, I'm beat = very tired; UK gutted = very disappointed, knackered = very tired, chuffed = very pleased, cheers = thanks / bye; UK/AU mate = friend; No way! = I can't believe it (or definitely not). Register: understand them, say them with friends if you like, never write them in work emails. Indonesian bridge: nggak tau, gimana, udah, makasih; 'terus dia kayak, "Hah?"' = the same quotative.

Overlapping talk: four strategies. (1) Follow the main thread: what is the group deciding (where, when, who)? Note each proposal and what happens to it. (2) Turn-taking cues: giving the turn (Sorry, go on / No, you go / Go ahead / After you), taking it (Sorry, can I just… / Can I jump in? / Hang on / Wait, wait), keeping it (Let me just finish / Hold on, I haven't finished), returning (As I was saying… / Anyway…). (3) Back-channelling (mm, mm-hm, uh-huh, yeah, right, I see) = I'm listening, not I agree; real agreement = Good idea / Sounds good / I'm with you / Fair enough. (4) Unfinished sentences usually come back after the interruption; the DECISION is the last proposal someone accepts (Let's go with… / OK, X then / X it is / Done / Agreed). Ask who decides and what was decided, not who spoke first or most.

Films, series and stand-up: subtitles plan = English subtitles first (not Indonesian), then rewatch short scenes without, replay 10 seconds of what you missed, say the line aloud; choose everyday-talk shows with recurring characters (sitcoms, workplace dramas) before noisy action films; subtitles often shorten speech and drop fillers. Jokes are hard because of cultural references, wordplay/puns (one word, two meanings), timing (the pause before the punchline) and callbacks (an earlier joke returning), plus irony/understatement from C1. Stand-up structure: setup (builds an expectation) → punchline (breaks it, usually the last word); rule of three (two normal items, a surprising third). British humour tends towards irony, understatement, deadpan and self-mockery; American humour is often more direct and energetic with big exaggeration: tendencies only. Indonesian stand-up uses the same setup–punchline shape.

Common errors to target: waiting for every word to come out clearly and getting lost; not recognising lemme/whaddya/dunno; hearing 'I was gonna call' as 'I will call' or 'I called'; taking like as 'suka'; reading US 'I'm down' as 'sad'; treating mm-hm/yeah/right as agreement (Indonesian 'iya, iya' works the same way); reporting the first proposal or the loudest speaker as the decision; watching only with Indonesian subtitles; translating puns word by word; writing gonna/dunno/kinda in emails. Limits: at C2 any grammar is fine, but keep listen texts natural and one speaker. Answers are short (a full form, a name, a place, a punchline word): accept the meaning. Only test clear cases.

keyPoints.title: Fast speech: reduced forms, fillers and slang
keyPoints.explanation: Fast speakers squeeze words together: kinda = kind of, dunno = don't know, lemme = let me, gimme = give me, whaddya = what do you, d'you = do you, gotcha = I understand. I was gonna = I planned to, but didn't. Fillers and vague words (like, you know, sort of, and stuff, or whatever) carry little meaning: let them pass. He's like… / she goes… = he said / she said. Slang depends on the country: US I'm down = I'll join (not sad!), UK gutted = very disappointed. Understand them all; write them only in chats with friends.

examples.id: Nggak tahu, agak jauh sih. (dunno = don't know, kinda = kind of)

examples.en: I was gonna text you, but my phone died.
examples.id: Tadinya aku mau kirim pesan, tapi HP-ku mati. (jadi dia tidak mengirim pesan)
Karaoke habis kerja? Aku ikut! (slang US: bukan 'sedih')

id.title: Ucapan cepat: bentuk ringkas, kata pengisi dan slang
id.explanation: Penutur yang bicara cepat memadatkan kata-kata: kinda = kind of (agak), dunno = don't know, lemme = let me, gimme = give me, whaddya = what do you, d'you = do you, gotcha = aku paham. I was gonna = tadinya mau, tapi tidak jadi. Kata pengisi dan kata samar (like, you know, sort of, and stuff, or whatever) hampir tidak membawa makna: biarkan lewat. He's like… / she goes… = dia bilang. Slang bergantung pada negaranya: I'm down (US) = aku ikut (bukan sedih!), gutted (UK) = kecewa berat. Pahami semuanya; tulis hanya di obrolan dengan teman.

keyPoints.title: Following people who talk over each other
keyPoints.explanation: In real talk people interrupt, start together and stop in the middle of a sentence (— in a transcript). Follow the main thread: what is the group deciding? Use the turn-taking cues: Sorry, go on / No, you go = giving the turn; Can I just… / Hang on = taking it. Mm-hm, yeah, right, uh-huh only mean 'I'm listening', not 'I agree'. The decision is the last proposal that someone accepts: Let's go with…, OK, Thursday then, Thursday it is.

examples.en: Sorry, can I just jump in here?
examples.id: Maaf, boleh aku menyela sebentar? (mengambil giliran)

id.title: Mengikuti orang yang bicara tumpang tindih
id.explanation: Dalam obrolan nyata orang saling memotong, mulai bicara bersamaan dan berhenti di tengah kalimat (— di transkrip). Ikuti alur utamanya: apa yang sedang diputuskan kelompok itu? Pakai penanda giliran bicara: Sorry, go on / No, you go = memberi giliran; Can I just… / Hang on = mengambil giliran. Mm-hm, yeah, right, uh-huh hanya berarti 'aku mendengarkan', bukan 'aku setuju'. Keputusannya adalah usulan terakhir yang diterima seseorang: Let's go with…, OK, Thursday then, Thursday it is.

keyPoints.title: Films, series and stand-up comedy
keyPoints.explanation: Watch with English subtitles first (not Indonesian), then rewatch short scenes without them and replay what you missed. Jokes get lost through cultural references, wordplay (one word, two meanings), timing (a pause before the punchline) and callbacks (an earlier joke that comes back). A stand-up joke has a setup that builds an expectation and a punchline that breaks it, usually with the last word. British humour leans on irony, understatement and deadpan; American humour is often more direct and energetic. These are tendencies, not rules.

examples.en: My new phone has face recognition. Every morning it looks at me and asks for my password.
examples.id: HP baruku punya pengenal wajah. Tiap pagi dia menatapku lalu minta kata sandi. (punchline: password: wajah pagiku tidak dikenali)

examples.en: The intern asked where the minutes of the meeting were. I said, 'Somewhere between hour one and hour three.'
examples.id: Anak magang bertanya di mana notulen rapatnya. Kujawab, 'Di antara jam pertama dan jam ketiga.' (permainan kata: minutes = notulen, juga menit)

id.title: Film, serial dan stand-up comedy
id.explanation: Tonton dengan subtitel bahasa Inggris dulu (bukan bahasa Indonesia), lalu tonton ulang adegan pendek tanpa subtitel dan putar ulang bagian yang terlewat. Lelucon sering tidak tertangkap karena rujukan budaya, permainan kata (satu kata, dua makna), timing (jeda sebelum punchline) dan callback (lelucon sebelumnya yang muncul lagi). Lelucon stand-up punya setup (pengantar) yang membangun harapan dan punchline (pamungkas) yang mematahkannya, biasanya dengan kata terakhir. Humor British cenderung memakai ironi, understatement dan deadpan (wajah datar); humor Amerika sering lebih langsung dan bersemangat. Ini kecenderungan, bukan aturan.

guidedPractice.prompt: Your friend sends a voice note: 'Gimme a sec, I'm parking.' Write 'gimme a sec' in full words.
guidedPractice.hint: gimme is two words squeezed together: a verb + me. And sec is short for a unit of time.

guidedPractice.prompt: Rina tells a story: 'So I showed him the bill, and he's like, "That's not mine."' What does 'he's like' mean here? Answer in two or three words.
guidedPractice.hint: Here like isn't 'suka'. It introduces the words someone said, like Indonesian 'terus dia kayak, "…"'.

guidedPractice.prompt: In a meeting, you and Dimas start speaking at the same time. He stops and says: 'No, no, you go.' What should you do?
expected: say what i wanted to say
guidedPractice.hint: 'You go' gives you the turn: he's letting you speak first.

guidedPractice.prompt: Near the end of her show, a comedian repeats a line from a joke she told much earlier, and the audience laughs even harder. What is this kind of joke called?

independentPractice.prompt: Your American colleague writes in the team chat: 'My bad, I sent the wrong file.' What does 'my bad' mean?
independentPractice.hint: It's US slang to admit something you did wrong, quickly and informally.

independentPractice.prompt: On a call, while Pak Hasan explains his plan, Sari keeps saying 'Mm-hm… yeah… right.' At the end she says: 'Sorry, I'm not convinced.' Does Sari agree with the plan? Answer yes or no.
independentPractice.hint: Mm-hm, yeah and right while someone talks mean 'I'm listening'. Her real view comes at the end.

independentPractice.prompt: You're watching a British series with Indonesian subtitles to improve your listening. Which subtitles should you switch to first?
independentPractice.hint: You want to hear and read the same words at the same time.

assessment.prompt: In a series, a character hears that her flatmate has sold her car. She shouts: 'Whaddya mean, you sold my car?' Write 'whaddya' in full words.
assessment.rubric: Correct: what do you (Whaddya mean? = What do you mean?). 'what do' or 'what you' (one word missing) = 50. 'what are you' = 30 (whaddya can mean that before an -ing form, as in whaddya doing?, but 'What are you mean' isn't English). 'what did you' = 50 (possible in very fast speech, but the present 'mean' shows do). Anything else = 0.

assessment.prompt: Your colleague Budi leaves you a voice message. Listen. What does he want you to do? Answer in English in a few words.
assessment.listen: Hey, it's Budi. I was gonna call the supplier this afternoon, but I'm kinda swamped with the audit. Could you call them for me? Their number's in the shared folder. Thanks!
acceptableAnswers: call the supplier instead of him
assessment.rubric: Correct: call (phone, contact) the supplier. 'I was gonna call' = Budi planned to call, but he's too busy (kinda swamped = rather overloaded), so he asks you. 'find the number' / 'look in the shared folder' = 40 (a detail, not the request). 'Budi will call the supplier' = 0 (misreads was gonna as a plan that still stands). 'help with the audit' = 20.

assessment.prompt: Tom, your British colleague, watched his football team lose the cup final on penalties last night. This morning he says: 'I'm absolutely gutted.' How does he feel? Write one word in English.
assessment.rubric: Correct: (very) disappointed (UK slang gutted = extremely disappointed, devastated). 'sad' / 'upset' = 70 (the right direction, but weaker). The idea in Indonesian (kecewa berat) = 60. 'angry' = 30. 'tired' = 0 (that's knackered). 'hungry' / 'sick' = 0 (literal readings of gut). 'happy' = 0.

assessment.prompt:
Read this transcript of a project meeting at a Jakarta startup (— = the speaker is cut off).

Bu Ani: Right, the launch. I'd say Monday the fifth, because —
Dimas: Sorry, sorry, can I just — the fifth? The payment page won't be —
Bu Ani: No, go on.
Dimas: It won't be ready till the twelfth. Realistically.
Rina: Mm. Yeah.
Bu Ani: OK. The twelfth, then. Rina, can you let the client know?
Rina: Will do.

Who makes the final decision about the launch date? Write the name.
assessment.rubric: Correct: Bu Ani ('OK. The twelfth, then.' is the decision; she also gives Rina the next task). 'Dimas' = 30 (he interrupts with the information that changes the date, but he doesn't decide; 'No, go on' only gives him the turn). 'Rina' = 0 ('Mm. Yeah.' is back-channelling; she only informs the client). 'the twelfth' / '12' = 20 (the decision, not who made it).

assessment.prompt:
Read this transcript of a team call about the end-of-year outing (— = the speaker is cut off).

Sari: So for the outing, what about Puncak? We could —
Budi: Mm-hm.
Sari: — rent a villa for the weekend.
Budi: Yeah. Only — sorry — half the team has kids. A whole weekend's hard.
Dimas: What about one day in Kota Tua? Back home by six.
Sari: Hm. Fair enough. Kota Tua it is.
Budi: Perfect.

Where will the team go? Write the place.
assessment.rubric: Correct: Kota Tua ('Kota Tua it is' = the decision; Budi's 'Perfect' agrees). 'Puncak' = 0 (Sari's first idea: Budi's 'Mm-hm' and 'Yeah' are back-channelling, and then he raises a problem). 'a villa' = 0. 'home' = 0.

assessment.prompt: This is an original practice joke from a stand-up set: 'I finally organised my whole life in a spreadsheet. It's got one column: Later.' Which word is the punchline? Write the word.
assessment.rubric: Correct: later (the setup, 'organised my whole life in a spreadsheet', makes you expect a well-planned life; the last word shows that everything is simply postponed). 'spreadsheet' / 'column' / 'organised' = 20 (part of the setup that builds the expectation).

assessment.prompt: Original practice joke: 'I told my boss I needed a day off to recharge. So he gave me a phone charger.' The joke plays on one word with two meanings. Which word is it? Write it.
assessment.rubric: Correct: recharge (for a person: rest and get your energy back; for a device: fill the battery again; the boss pretends to take the second meaning). 'charger' = 60 (it points to the pun, but the word with two meanings is recharge). 'day off' / 'boss' = 0.

blocks.text:
**Quick recap:** at B2 you met sounds that disappear and change (*last night* → 'las night', *would you* → 'wouldja') and *gonna / wanna / gotta*; at C1 you learnt to ignore fillers and to keep the last version after a self-correction. Now the speed goes up. In films, series, podcasts and chats with friends, whole groups of words melt into one **reduced form** (a few words said so fast that they sound like one word):
- *kinda* = kind of (agak), *sorta* = sort of
- *dunno* = don't know
- *lemme* = let me, *gimme* = give me
- *whaddya* = what do you (*Whaddya think?*); sometimes what are you (*Whaddya doing?*)
- *d'you* = do you (*D'you want some?*), *ya* = you, *y'know* = you know
- *gotcha* = I understand / got you, *c'mon* = come on, *'cause* or *cuz* = because
- very casual American: *Jeet?* = Did you eat?

**One trap: *was gonna*.** *I was gonna call you* = I planned to call you, **but I didn't**. The plan changed, and the speaker usually says why straight after (*…but my battery died*). It's not a future plan any more.

**How to listen:** catch the stressed words first (*call*, *battery*, *died*), then rebuild the small words from grammar and context, as you did at B2.

id.text:
**Ingat lagi sebentar:** di B2 kamu bertemu bunyi yang hilang dan berubah (*last night* → 'las night', *would you* → 'wouldja') serta *gonna / wanna / gotta*; di C1 kamu belajar mengabaikan kata pengisi dan memegang versi terakhir setelah koreksi diri. Sekarang kecepatannya naik. Di film, serial, podcast dan obrolan dengan teman, beberapa kata sekaligus melebur jadi satu **bentuk ringkas** (reduced form: beberapa kata yang diucapkan begitu cepat sampai terdengar seperti satu kata):
- *kinda* = kind of (agak), *sorta* = sort of
- *dunno* = don't know (nggak tahu)
- *lemme* = let me (biar aku), *gimme* = give me (kasih aku)
- *whaddya* = what do you (*Whaddya think?* = menurutmu?); kadang what are you (*Whaddya doing?* = lagi ngapain?)
- *d'you* = do you (*D'you want some?* = mau?), *ya* = you, *y'know* = you know
- *gotcha* = aku paham / oke, *c'mon* = come on (ayo), *'cause* atau *cuz* = because (karena)
- Amerika yang sangat santai: *Jeet?* = Did you eat? (udah makan?)

**Satu jebakan: *was gonna*.** *I was gonna call you* = tadinya aku mau meneleponmu, **tapi tidak jadi**. Rencananya berubah, dan biasanya pembicara langsung menyebut alasannya (*…but my battery died*). Ini bukan rencana masa depan lagi.

**Cara menyimak:** tangkap dulu kata-kata yang ditekan (*call*, *battery*, *died*), lalu susun kembali kata-kata kecilnya dari tata bahasa dan konteks, seperti di B2.

rows.note: dunno = don't know · kinda = kind of

id.note: dunno = don't know · kinda = kind of (agak)

rows.en: Whaddya think of the new office?
I was gonna text you, but my phone died.
rows.id: Tadinya aku mau kirim pesan, tapi HP-ku mati.
rows.note: was gonna = planned to, but didn't

id.note: was gonna = tadinya mau, tapi tidak jadi

blocks.text: **You already do this in Indonesian.** In a relaxed chat nobody says *tidak tahu, bagaimana, sudah, terima kasih*: you hear *nggak tau, gimana, udah, makasih*. English is the same, and textbooks show neither. Two traps: waiting for every word to come out clearly (it won't, and you get lost), and copying these forms into writing. Hear them and understand them; say them with friends if you like; never write *gonna, dunno, kinda* in an email to a client, lecturer or manager. **Honest note:** the app's audio is one calm voice at normal speed, so it can't sound like a fast film. Here you learn what to listen for; real speed comes from the shows and podcasts you watch (see the resources).

id.text: **Sebenarnya kamu sudah melakukan ini dalam bahasa Indonesia.** Dalam obrolan santai tidak ada yang bilang *tidak tahu, bagaimana, sudah, terima kasih*: yang terdengar *nggak tau, gimana, udah, makasih*. Bahasa Inggris juga begitu, dan buku pelajaran tidak menunjukkan keduanya. Dua jebakan: menunggu setiap kata terdengar jelas (tidak akan terjadi, dan kamu jadi tertinggal), dan menyalin bentuk-bentuk ini ke tulisan. Dengar dan pahami; ucapkan bersama teman kalau mau; jangan pernah menulis *gonna, dunno, kinda* di email untuk klien, dosen atau manajer. **Catatan jujur:** audio aplikasi ini satu suara yang tenang dengan kecepatan normal, jadi tidak bisa terdengar seperti film yang cepat. Di sini kamu belajar apa yang perlu didengarkan; kecepatan asli datang dari tontonan dan podcast yang kamu ikuti (lihat sumber belajarnya).

blocks.prompt: A friend says: 'I was gonna come to your party, but my flight got delayed.' Did she come to the party?
options: No: she planned to come, but she didn't.
Not yet: she's going to come next time.
blocks.explain: *was gonna* = was going to = planned to. The *but* that follows tells you the plan didn't happen: the delayed flight stopped her. It isn't a promise for next time.

id.prompt: Seorang teman berkata: 'I was gonna come to your party, but my flight got delayed.' Apakah dia datang ke pestamu?
id.explain: *was gonna* = was going to = tadinya mau. Kata *but* sesudahnya memberitahumu rencananya tidak terjadi: penerbangannya tertunda. Ini bukan janji untuk lain kali.

material.title: Fillers, vague words and film slang

blocks.text:
Fast speakers also fill their sentences with words that carry **little meaning**. Let them pass, but know what they do:
- **Fillers** (words that give the speaker time or keep the turn): *like, you know, I mean, well, basically*. *She was, like, really upset* = she was really upset.
- **Vague language** (deliberately not exact): *and stuff, and that* (UK), *or whatever, or something, sort of, kind of*, *-ish* (*sevenish* = about seven), *a bunch of* (US = a lot of).
- **Quotatives** (words that introduce what someone said): *be like* and *go*. *And he's like, 'Seriously?'* = and he said (or reacted): 'Seriously?'. *Then she goes, 'No way.'* = then she said. This *like* has nothing to do with *suka*.
- **Intensifiers**: *literally* often just means 'really' (*I literally died* = I was very embarrassed, or I laughed a lot).

**Film slang** depends on the country and changes fast. Common ones:
- US: *I'm down* = I'm in, I'll join; *my bad* = my mistake; *bail (on someone)* = cancel or leave suddenly; *I'm beat* = very tired.
- UK: *gutted* = very disappointed; *knackered* = very tired; *chuffed* = very pleased; *cheers* = thanks (or bye).
- UK and Australia: *mate* = friend. Everywhere: *No way!* = I can't believe it (or: definitely not).

id.text:
Penutur yang cepat juga mengisi kalimatnya dengan kata-kata yang **hampir tidak bermakna**. Biarkan lewat, tapi kenali fungsinya:
- **Kata pengisi** (filler: kata yang memberi waktu berpikir atau menahan giliran bicara): *like, you know, I mean, well, basically*. *She was, like, really upset* = dia benar-benar kesal.
- **Bahasa samar** (vague language: sengaja tidak persis): *and stuff, and that* (UK) = dan lain-lain, *or whatever, or something* = atau apalah, *sort of, kind of* = agak, *-ish* (*sevenish* = sekitar jam tujuh), *a bunch of* (US) = banyak.
- **Pengantar kutipan** (quotative: kata yang mengantar ucapan orang): *be like* dan *go*. *And he's like, 'Seriously?'* = terus dia bilang (atau bereaksi): 'Serius?'. *Then she goes, 'No way.'* = lalu dia bilang. *Like* ini tidak ada hubungannya dengan *suka*. Bahasa Indonesia melakukan hal yang sama persis: *terus dia kayak, 'Hah?'*
- **Penguat** (intensifier): *literally* sering hanya berarti 'benar-benar' (*I literally died* = aku malu banget, atau aku ketawa banget).

**Slang film** bergantung pada negaranya dan cepat berubah. Yang umum:
- US: *I'm down* = aku ikut; *my bad* = salahku; *bail (on someone)* = batal atau pergi mendadak; *I'm beat* = capek banget.
- UK: *gutted* = kecewa berat; *knackered* = capek banget; *chuffed* = senang sekali; *cheers* = makasih (atau dah).
- UK dan Australia: *mate* = teman. Di mana-mana: *No way!* = nggak mungkin! / masa sih! (atau: sama sekali tidak).

rows.en: We could get snacks or whatever.
rows.id: Kita bisa beli camilan atau apalah.

rows.en: Sorry, my bad. I sent you the old file.
rows.id: Maaf, salahku. Aku mengirim file yang lama.

rows.en: I'm knackered. Let's leave at eightish.
rows.id: Aku capek banget. Ayo pulang sekitar jam delapan.
rows.note: UK slang: very tired · eightish = about eight

id.note: slang UK: capek banget · eightish = sekitar jam delapan

blocks.text: **Two traps for Indonesian learners.** First: *I'm down* (US slang) means *I'll join*, but *I'm feeling down* means *I'm sad*: one small word changes everything, so use the context (an invitation + *I'm down* = yes). Second: *like* in fast speech is usually not *suka*: it's a filler, or it introduces what someone said. Slang also ages quickly: a film from 2005 may use words young people don't say any more. When a word is new, check it after the scene in a learner's dictionary (Cambridge, Oxford Learner's), which marks it *informal*, *UK* or *US*.

id.text: **Dua jebakan untuk pembelajar Indonesia.** Pertama: *I'm down* (slang US) berarti *aku ikut*, tapi *I'm feeling down* berarti *aku sedih*: satu kata kecil mengubah semuanya, jadi pakai konteksnya (ajakan + *I'm down* = mau). Kedua: *like* dalam ucapan cepat biasanya bukan *suka*: itu kata pengisi, atau pengantar ucapan seseorang. Slang juga cepat usang: film tahun 2005 bisa memakai kata yang sudah tidak dipakai anak muda sekarang. Kalau ada kata baru, cek setelah adegannya di kamus pembelajar (Cambridge, Oxford Learner's), yang menandainya *informal*, *UK* atau *US*.

blocks.prompt: In a series, a character tells her friends: 'So I asked for a refund, and the manager goes, "Not today, madam."' What does 'goes' mean here?
blocks.explain: *go* (and *be like*) can introduce what someone said: *the manager goes, '…'* = the manager says. The quote straight after it is the clue. It has nothing to do with walking or leaving.

id.prompt: Dalam sebuah serial, seorang tokoh bercerita kepada teman-temannya: 'So I asked for a refund, and the manager goes, "Not today, madam."' Apa arti 'goes' di sini?
id.explain: *go* (dan *be like*) bisa mengantar ucapan seseorang: *the manager goes, '…'* = manajernya bilang. Kutipan tepat sesudahnya adalah petunjuknya. Ini tidak ada hubungannya dengan berjalan atau pergi.

material.title: When people talk over each other

blocks.text:
In a lecture one person speaks; at a family dinner, on a team call or in a sitcom, everyone does. People **interrupt**, start at the same time, stop in the middle of a sentence and finish it later, or let someone else finish it. In a transcript, **—** shows a cut-off and **…** a sentence that trails away.

**Four strategies:**
1. **Follow the main thread** (the question the group is trying to answer: where, when, who?). Note each proposal and what happens to it.
2. **Use the turn-taking cues** (words that pass the turn to speak). Giving the turn: *Sorry, go on. / No, you go. / Go ahead. / After you.* Taking it: *Sorry, can I just… / Can I jump in? / Hang on. / Wait, wait.* Keeping it: *Let me just finish. / Hold on, I haven't finished.* Coming back: *As I was saying… / Anyway…*
3. **Back-channelling is not agreement.** *Mm, mm-hm, uh-huh, yeah, right, I see* said while someone else talks usually mean 'I'm listening, carry on'. Real agreement sounds like *Good idea. / Sounds good. / I'm with you on that. / Fair enough.*
4. **Unfinished sentences:** don't panic. The idea usually comes back after the interruption (*We could — / Mm-hm. / — book the big room*). The **decision** is the last proposal that someone accepts: *Let's go with… / OK, Thursday then. / Thursday it is. / Done. / Agreed.* It's the C1 rule again: the last version is the fact.

id.text:
Di kuliah, satu orang yang bicara; di makan malam keluarga, rapat tim online atau sitkom, semua orang bicara. Orang **saling memotong** (interrupt), mulai bicara bersamaan, berhenti di tengah kalimat lalu menyelesaikannya nanti, atau membiarkan orang lain yang menyelesaikannya. Di transkrip, **—** menandai kalimat yang terpotong dan **…** kalimat yang menggantung.

**Empat strategi:**
1. **Ikuti alur utamanya** (pertanyaan yang sedang dijawab kelompok itu: di mana, kapan, siapa?). Catat setiap usulan dan apa yang terjadi padanya.
2. **Pakai penanda giliran bicara** (kata-kata yang mengoper giliran). Memberi giliran: *Sorry, go on. / No, you go. / Go ahead. / After you.* (silakan, kamu duluan). Mengambil giliran: *Sorry, can I just… / Can I jump in? / Hang on. / Wait, wait.* (maaf, boleh aku… / sebentar). Menahan giliran: *Let me just finish. / Hold on, I haven't finished.* (biar kuselesaikan dulu). Kembali ke topik: *As I was saying… / Anyway…* (seperti tadi kubilang…).
3. **Back-channelling bukan tanda setuju.** *Mm, mm-hm, uh-huh, yeah, right, I see* yang diucapkan saat orang lain bicara biasanya berarti 'aku mendengarkan, lanjutkan' (seperti *hmm, iya, oh gitu* dalam bahasa Indonesia). Setuju yang sungguhan terdengar seperti *Good idea. / Sounds good. / I'm with you on that. / Fair enough.*
4. **Kalimat yang tidak selesai:** jangan panik. Idenya biasanya kembali setelah interupsi (*We could — / Mm-hm. / — book the big room*). **Keputusannya** adalah usulan terakhir yang diterima seseorang: *Let's go with… / OK, Thursday then. / Thursday it is. / Done. / Agreed.* Ini aturan C1 lagi: versi terakhir adalah faktanya.

rows.en: Sorry, can I just jump in here?
Hold on, let me just finish.
OK, the Padang place it is.
rows.id: Oke, jadi ke rumah makan Padang.

blocks.text: **The Indonesian trap:** *iya, iya* while someone talks often just means 'I'm following', and English *yeah, right* works the same way. Learners who hear *yeah* as *yes, I agree* report the wrong decision. Wait for the agreement words or the decision phrase. **Honest note about practice:** our audio is one voice, so it can't overlap. In this lesson you practise with written transcripts; for real overlapping talk, watch sitcoms, panel shows and family dramas with English subtitles, and try the 'Birthday parties' recording in the resources (three friends cutting each other off).

id.text: **Jebakan untuk orang Indonesia:** *iya, iya* saat orang lain bicara sering hanya berarti 'aku mengikuti', dan *yeah, right* dalam bahasa Inggris bekerja dengan cara yang sama. Pembelajar yang mendengar *yeah* sebagai *ya, aku setuju* akan melaporkan keputusan yang salah. Tunggu kata-kata persetujuan atau frasa keputusannya. **Catatan jujur soal latihan:** audio kami satu suara, jadi tidak bisa tumpang tindih. Di pelajaran ini kamu berlatih dengan transkrip tertulis; untuk obrolan tumpang tindih yang sungguhan, tonton sitkom, acara panel dan drama keluarga dengan subtitel bahasa Inggris, dan coba rekaman 'Birthday parties' di sumber belajar (tiga teman yang saling memotong).

blocks.prompt: While you explain your plan on a call, Pak Hasan keeps saying 'Mm-hm… right… yeah.' What does this tell you for sure?
options: He wants you to stop talking.
blocks.explain: *Mm-hm, right, yeah* while someone talks are back-channelling: they show he's following and you can carry on. They don't show agreement: wait for words like *Sounds good* or *Let's do that*. They don't ask you to stop either: that would be *Hang on* or *Can I just…*.

id.prompt: Saat kamu menjelaskan rencanamu di telepon, Pak Hasan terus berkata 'Mm-hm… right… yeah.' Apa yang pasti bisa kamu simpulkan?
id.explain: *Mm-hm, right, yeah* saat orang lain bicara adalah back-channelling: tanda bahwa ia mengikuti dan kamu boleh lanjut. Itu bukan tanda setuju: tunggu kata-kata seperti *Sounds good* atau *Let's do that*. Itu juga bukan permintaan berhenti: untuk itu orang bilang *Hang on* atau *Can I just…*.

material.title: Films and series: a subtitles plan

blocks.text:
Films and series are the best listening practice there is, and the hardest: fast speech, slang, background noise, music, accents and several people at once. A plan that works:
1. **English subtitles first, not Indonesian.** With Indonesian subtitles you read Indonesian and your ears switch off. English subtitles let you hear and read the **same** words, so you learn what *gonna* or *whaddya* sounds like and how the full words are written.
2. **Then rewatch a scene without subtitles.** A 2–3 minute scene you already understand is perfect.
3. **Replay what you missed.** Go back 10 seconds, guess the words, then check with the subtitles. If you knew the words but didn't hear them, it was a reduced form or linking: say the line aloud yourself.
4. **Choose the right shows.** Start with lots of everyday talk and the same characters every episode (sitcoms, family and workplace dramas): you tune in to their voices. Action films full of noise and music are harder. Mix British and American shows.

Good to know: subtitles often **shorten** what people say and leave out fillers and repetition, so don't worry if they don't match every word.

id.text:
Film dan serial adalah latihan menyimak terbaik, sekaligus yang paling sulit: ucapan cepat, slang, suara latar, musik, aksen dan beberapa orang bicara sekaligus. Rencana yang berhasil:
1. **Subtitel bahasa Inggris dulu, bukan bahasa Indonesia.** Dengan subtitel bahasa Indonesia kamu membaca bahasa Indonesia dan telingamu berhenti bekerja. Subtitel bahasa Inggris membuatmu mendengar dan membaca kata-kata yang **sama**, jadi kamu belajar bunyi *gonna* atau *whaddya* dan cara menulis kata lengkapnya.
2. **Lalu tonton ulang satu adegan tanpa subtitel.** Adegan 2–3 menit yang sudah kamu pahami itu pas sekali.
3. **Putar ulang yang terlewat.** Mundur 10 detik, tebak kata-katanya, lalu cek dengan subtitel. Kalau kamu tahu katanya tapi tidak menangkap bunyinya, itu bentuk ringkas atau sambungan bunyi: ucapkan kalimatnya sendiri dengan suara keras.
4. **Pilih tontonan yang tepat.** Mulai dari yang banyak obrolan sehari-hari dan tokohnya sama setiap episode (sitkom, drama keluarga dan drama kantor): telingamu jadi terbiasa dengan suara mereka. Film laga yang penuh suara dan musik lebih sulit. Campur tontonan British dan Amerika.

Perlu diketahui: subtitel sering **memendekkan** ucapan dan membuang kata pengisi dan pengulangan, jadi jangan khawatir kalau tidak cocok kata per kata.

blocks.text: **Be honest with yourself:** this app trains **what** to listen for, but listening at native speed only grows with hours of real input. A little every day beats a whole film once a month. Watch actively for part of the time (pause, replay, note 5–6 new phrases a week), then enjoy an episode just for fun.

id.text: **Jujurlah pada dirimu sendiri:** aplikasi ini melatih **apa** yang perlu didengarkan, tapi kemampuan menyimak dengan kecepatan asli hanya tumbuh dari berjam-jam masukan nyata. Sedikit setiap hari lebih baik daripada satu film penuh sebulan sekali. Tonton secara aktif sebagian waktunya (jeda, putar ulang, catat 5–6 frasa baru per minggu), lalu nikmati satu episode sekadar untuk hiburan.

blocks.prompt: Dimas wants to train his listening with a British series. Which plan works best?
options: Watch every episode with Indonesian subtitles.
Watch with no subtitles from the start and never replay anything.
Watch with English subtitles first, then rewatch key scenes without subtitles.
blocks.explain: English subtitles let him hear and read the same words; rewatching without them then trains the ear. With Indonesian subtitles he mostly reads Indonesian. No subtitles and no replays from the start usually means he misses too much to learn from it.

id.prompt: Dimas ingin melatih kemampuan menyimaknya dengan sebuah serial British. Rencana mana yang paling berhasil?
id.explain: Subtitel bahasa Inggris membuatnya mendengar dan membaca kata-kata yang sama; menonton ulang tanpa subtitel lalu melatih telinganya. Dengan subtitel bahasa Indonesia dia lebih banyak membaca bahasa Indonesia. Tanpa subtitel dan tanpa putar ulang sejak awal biasanya membuatnya melewatkan terlalu banyak untuk bisa belajar.

material.title: Why jokes are hard, and how stand-up works

blocks.text:
You can understand every word and still miss the joke. The usual reasons:
- **Cultural references:** a TV show, a politician, a shop or an event the audience knows. Fix: note it and look it up after the scene.
- **Wordplay** (a *pun*): one word with two meanings. Practice joke: *The intern asked where the minutes of the meeting were. I said, 'Somewhere between hour one and hour three.'* (*minutes* = notulen, but also menit.)
- **Timing:** a short pause just before the punchline. In text we show it with … or |.
- **Callbacks:** a joke that comes back later in the show. Practice example: early on, a comedian says her mother phones every day only to ask *Sudah makan?* Forty minutes later she tells a story about a police officer who stops her car, looks at her licence and asks… *Sudah makan?* The second laugh is bigger, because the audience remembers.
- **Irony and understatement** (from C1): *Well, that went well* after a disaster.

**How a stand-up joke works:** the **setup** builds an expectation; the **punchline** breaks it, usually with the **last word**. *My new phone has face recognition* (you expect: it recognises me). *Every morning it looks at me and asks for my password* (it doesn't recognise my morning face). Another common shape is the **rule of three**: two normal items, then a surprising third.

**British vs American humour (tendencies, with many exceptions):** British comedy often uses irony, understatement, **deadpan** (saying something absurd with a completely straight face) and self-mockery about failure and awkward moments. American comedy is often more direct and energetic, with big exaggeration and confident storytelling. Indonesian stand-up uses the same setup–punchline shape, so you already know how it works.

id.text:
Kamu bisa paham setiap kata tapi tetap tidak menangkap leluconnya. Penyebab yang biasa:
- **Rujukan budaya** (cultural reference): acara TV, politikus, toko atau peristiwa yang dikenal penonton. Solusinya: catat dan cari tahu setelah adegannya.
- **Permainan kata** (wordplay, *pun* / plesetan): satu kata dengan dua makna. Lelucon latihan: *The intern asked where the minutes of the meeting were. I said, 'Somewhere between hour one and hour three.'* (*minutes* = notulen, tapi juga menit.)
- **Timing:** jeda pendek tepat sebelum punchline. Di teks kami menandainya dengan … atau |.
- **Callback:** lelucon yang muncul lagi di bagian akhir pertunjukan. Contoh latihan: di awal, seorang komika bercerita ibunya menelepon setiap hari hanya untuk bertanya *Sudah makan?* Empat puluh menit kemudian dia bercerita tentang polisi yang menghentikan mobilnya, melihat SIM-nya lalu bertanya… *Sudah makan?* Tawa kedua lebih besar, karena penonton ingat.
- **Ironi dan understatement** (dari C1): *Well, that went well* (yah, lancar sekali) setelah kekacauan.

**Cara kerja lelucon stand-up:** **setup** (pengantar) membangun harapan; **punchline** (pamungkas) mematahkannya, biasanya dengan **kata terakhir**. *My new phone has face recognition* (kamu menduga: HP-nya mengenaliku). *Every morning it looks at me and asks for my password* (wajah pagiku tidak dikenali). Bentuk lain yang umum adalah **rule of three** (aturan tiga): dua hal biasa, lalu hal ketiga yang mengejutkan.

**Humor British vs Amerika (kecenderungan, banyak pengecualian):** komedi British sering memakai ironi, understatement, **deadpan** (mengatakan hal yang absurd dengan wajah benar-benar datar) dan menertawakan diri sendiri soal kegagalan dan momen canggung. Komedi Amerika sering lebih langsung dan bersemangat, dengan pembesar-besaran dan cara bercerita yang percaya diri. Stand-up Indonesia memakai bentuk setup–punchline yang sama, jadi kamu sudah tahu cara kerjanya.

rows.en: My new phone has face recognition. Every morning it looks at me and asks for my password.
rows.id: HP baruku punya pengenal wajah. Tiap pagi dia menatapku lalu minta kata sandi.

id.note: setup: pengenal wajah · punchline: password (kata sandi)

rows.en: The intern asked where the minutes of the meeting were. I said, 'Somewhere between hour one and hour three.'
rows.id: Anak magang bertanya di mana notulen rapatnya. Kujawab, 'Di antara jam pertama dan jam ketiga.'
rows.note: pun: minutes = notes of a meeting / units of time

blocks.text: When the audience laughs and you don't, ask yourself: was it a reference, a pun, a callback or irony? Rewind and look at the **last few words**: that's usually the punchline. Don't translate jokes word by word into Indonesian: puns almost never survive translation.

id.text: Kalau penonton tertawa dan kamu tidak, tanyakan pada dirimu: apakah itu rujukan budaya, plesetan, callback atau ironi? Mundurkan dan perhatikan **beberapa kata terakhir**: biasanya itulah punchline-nya. Jangan menerjemahkan lelucon kata per kata ke bahasa Indonesia: plesetan hampir tidak pernah selamat dalam terjemahan.

blocks.prompt: Original practice joke: 'For my holiday in Bali I packed sunscreen, a hat and a laptop full of work I promised I'd finish.' Why is it funny?
options: The third item breaks the pattern: a holiday list ends with work.
It's a pun: the word 'hat' has two meanings.
It refers back to a joke told earlier in the show.
blocks.explain: This is the rule of three: sunscreen and a hat set up a normal holiday list, and the third item (work) breaks the expectation. 'hat' has only one meaning here, and nothing refers to an earlier joke, so it isn't a pun or a callback.

id.prompt: Lelucon latihan orisinal: 'For my holiday in Bali I packed sunscreen, a hat and a laptop full of work I promised I'd finish.' Kenapa ini lucu?
id.explain: Ini rule of three: tabir surya dan topi membangun daftar liburan yang normal, dan hal ketiga (pekerjaan) mematahkan harapan itu. 'hat' hanya punya satu makna di sini, dan tidak ada yang merujuk ke lelucon sebelumnya, jadi ini bukan plesetan atau callback.

resources.title: FAST ENGLISH: The #1 Secret is REDUCTIONS
resources.note: American English. Tom Kelly from Rachel's English shows how native speakers shrink small words (for the, and in the, gonna, wanna, gotta, 'cuz') with real clips from TED Talks and interviews, so even formal speech uses reduced forms. Pronunciation-focused: use it to train your ear.

id.note: Bahasa Inggris Amerika. Tom Kelly dari Rachel's English menunjukkan bagaimana penutur asli memadatkan kata-kata kecil (for the, and in the, gonna, wanna, gotta, 'cuz) dengan potongan asli dari TED Talks dan wawancara, jadi ucapan formal pun memakai bentuk ringkas. Fokusnya pelafalan: pakai untuk melatih telingamu.

resources.title: Birthday parties
resources.note: C1 listening, British English: three friends argue casually about whether to celebrate birthdays, cutting each other off, teasing and using informal words like 'Nah' and 'I dunno'. Practise following the main thread when people talk over each other. With a full transcript and tasks.

id.note: Menyimak C1, bahasa Inggris British: tiga teman berdebat santai soal perlu tidaknya merayakan ulang tahun, saling memotong, saling meledek dan memakai kata informal seperti 'Nah' dan 'I dunno'. Latihan mengikuti alur utama saat orang bicara tumpang tindih. Ada transkrip lengkap dan latihannya.

resources.title: Learn English with Movies and TV! | 5 Powerful Tips from a Master Teacher | Rachel's English
resources.note: American English. Five tips for learning from films and series: pick shows at your level, pause and replay 10 seconds, write down what you hear, check with English subtitles and keep a notebook of phrases. Her order starts without subtitles and switches English subtitles on for the bits you miss: a good next step once 'English subtitles first' feels easy.

id.note: Bahasa Inggris Amerika. Lima tips belajar dari film dan serial: pilih tontonan sesuai levelmu, jeda dan putar ulang 10 detik, tulis apa yang kamu dengar, cek dengan subtitel bahasa Inggris dan simpan buku catatan frasa. Urutannya dimulai tanpa subtitel lalu menyalakan subtitel bahasa Inggris untuk bagian yang terlewat: langkah lanjutan yang bagus setelah 'subtitel bahasa Inggris dulu' terasa mudah.

id.intro: Selamat datang di bahasa Inggris dengan kecepatan asli! Film, serial, podcast dan teman-teman di pesta tidak bicara seperti buku pelajaran: mereka bilang 'dunno' dan 'kinda', bicara tumpang tindih, dan membuat lelucon yang terdengar tapi tidak sepenuhnya kamu tangkap. Di pelajaran ini kamu belajar apa yang perlu didengarkan, supaya jam-jam yang kamu habiskan untuk menonton dan menyimak dalam bahasa Inggris berubah menjadi pemahaman yang sungguhan.

assessment.lns-2: Rekan kerjamu, Budi, meninggalkan pesan suara. Dengarkan. Apa yang dia minta kamu lakukan? Jawab dalam bahasa Inggris dengan beberapa kata.
assessment.lns-3: Tom, rekan kerjamu dari Inggris, menonton tim sepak bolanya kalah adu penalti di final piala tadi malam. Pagi ini dia berkata: 'I'm absolutely gutted.' Bagaimana perasaannya? Tulis satu kata dalam bahasa Inggris.

assessment.lns-7: Lelucon latihan orisinal: 'I told my boss I needed a day off to recharge. So he gave me a phone charger.' Lelucon ini bermain dengan satu kata yang punya dua makna. Kata apa itu? Tulis katanya.
